4.title: 8강 4번 (53P)
4.q3: 이 글의 주제를 한 문장으로 요약하면?
4.passage:
Children come by their excitement naturally. Until it gets crushed out of them in school, kids [[innately:본능적으로]] know how to have fun and love what they do.

(A) But as Csikszentmihalyi noted, “Most enjoyable activities are not natural; they demand an effort that initially one is [[reluctant:꺼리는]] to make.” Some activities will only [[engross:몰입하게 하다]] us if we take the trouble to pay close attention to them.

(B) Simply put, flow is when your concentration is such that you lose all sense of time and place. The experience is its own reward; its end goal or outcome is just the icing on the cake. The satisfactions that go with creating an inspired work of art or [[flawlessly:흠잡을 데 없이]] executing an athletic feat are easy enough to imagine.

(C) Give them a wooden stick and watch as they begin to play with it. Wait a while and ask them what it is. You will get answers like “It’s a car!” or “It’s a rocket!” Kids have an unlimited [[capacity:능력, 용량]] not just for fantasy and imagination but for engrossment, much as artists or athletes do when they are experiencing the mental state that my mentor Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi famously described as “flow.”
4.key_points: 이 글의 답은 C B A 순서야.

5.title: 8강 5번&6번 (54P)
5.q1: 문맥상 옳지 않은 선지와, 그 이유는?
5.passage: Parents as gardeners and children as flowers have been popular and fitting parenting [[analogies:유추]] for the years between birth and twelve. However, seeing our adolescent children as flowers somehow does not ring true. Their growth and development have a (a) different quality than the flowering plants of childhood. Eugene Schwartz writes of teenagers, “And what of the [[abnormal:비정상적인]], poisonous plant? Here we see a picture of adolescence!” Like weeds, our teens go through a period of growing (b) inward, turning away from the light, seeking to create a space within themselves that clearly says, “This is me!” Like weeds, young teenagers create a private, inner pocket; they turn back upon themselves, (c) revisiting what they had previously [[rejoiced in:~을 즐거워하다]], withdrawing from the forces of nature that had previously nurtured them. The [[dilemma:진퇴양난]] for the parent as gardener becomes a process of learning how to care for a weed, when all the experiences we have ever had with weeds (d) push us to spray them dead, dig them out, and throw them away. Many of us gain a [[therapeutic:치유의]] satisfaction from digging weeds in our gardens, ridding our flower beds of that [[gangly:키가 크고 마른]] plant that (e) refuses to grow like the other flowers; its leaves a little too sharp, its stem a bit too woody, its [[essence:본질]] too poisonous. Some days we all feel the urge to pull out the teenage weed by the roots and throw it out the window! But the feeding and caring of a teenage weed is a much more [[delicate:섬세한, 예민한]] bit of gardening. We are responsible for its care, its well-being, and its development.
5.key_points: 문맥상 옳지 않은 낱말을 찾는 문제고, 정답은 (c) 야.

6.passage: Awards can strengthen people’s [[commitment:헌신, 전념]] to the organization giving the award. The [[intrinsic:내재적인]] motivation to perform well and [[in the interest of:~를 위해서]] the employer is ① praised by the giver and hence reinforced. In contrast, when an attempt is made to measure performance by pay, this intrinsic work motivation may well be [[crowded out:밀려나다/배제되다]]. After all, performance pay may unintentionally ② signal that the ultimate goal of all [[endeavours:노력]] is to get money. All that matters is to reach the [[criteria:기준]] in order to get the bonus promised. The content of work becomes ③ primary. Employees [[are induced:유도되다]] to disregard everything not covered by the criteria imposed even if they know this is — ④ bad for the organization they work for. Moreover, employees promised bonuses have a strong [[incentive:장려책, 원동력]] to exploit the system. If shareholder value is used as the major criterion for CEOs, they may artificially increase this number by short-term [[manipulations:조작, 조종]] or by buying back shares. The resulting shareholder value then does not reflect the [[underlying:근본적인]] state of the corporation but may be ⑤ biased in favour of short-run effects.

8.title: 10강 3번 (64P)

8.passage:
The [[prevailing:지배적인]] explanation of human action was that people were “pushed” by their internal drives or “pulled” by external events.

The science of [[psychology:심리학]] has not always cared about individual styles of thinking, or about individual human action or the individual at all. Quite the opposite. When I was a graduate student in psychology, twenty-five years ago, psychological dilemmas involving individual choice were not explained the way they are today. ( ① ) At that time, people were assumed to be products of their environment. ( ② ) Though the details of the pushing and pulling depended on the particular theory you happened to hold, in outline all the [[fashionable: 유행하는]] theories agreed on this [[proposition:명제]]. ( ③ ) The Freudians held that unresolved childhood conflicts drove adult behavior. ( ④ ) The followers of B. F. Skinner held that behavior was repeated only when reinforced [[externally:외부적으로]]. ( ⑤ ) The ethologists held that behavior resulted from fixed action patterns determined by our genes, and the behaviorist followers of Clark Hull held that we were [[goaded:자극받은]] into action by the need to reduce drives and satisfy biological needs.

9.passage: Adults make their own decisions, and children have most of their decisions made for them. Teenagers, of course, are stuck somewhere in the middle. As they [[gradually:점차, 점진적으로]] gain more freedom, they must learn to plan what to do with that freedom. To [[equip:준비시키다]] them for this, they are [[poised:태세를 갖춘]] at the most exciting point in the story of human [[cerebral:대뇌의]] change — the human brain changes throughout life, but that change is most complex in the second decade. Recent scientific discoveries go a long way towards showing that [[adolescence:청소년기]] is, perhaps surprisingly, the high point of the human brain — when the brain is at its largest, most flexible, and most changeable. The teenage years are when our greatest [[asset:자산]] — our mind — is most strongly shaped. Change in the teenage body is important, but for humans, change in the brain is more important still.

13.passage: Free markets have [[undoubtedly:의심할 여지 없이]] delivered [[substantial:상당한]] benefits. Not only is there a logical link between [[capitalism:자본주의]] and [[liberty:자유]], but the [[discipline:규율]] given by the price mechanism filters out inefficient businesses and drives innovation. Industrial capitalism has generated a [[cornucopia:풍요로운 공급]] of material wealth unimaginable to previous generations, and its essentially [[decentralised:탈중심화된]] character most closely mirrors the vast [[emergent:떠오르는, 신흥의]] system that is the globalised world. As observed by Vaclav Havel, the Czech Republic’s first president following liberation from Soviet shackles, capitalism is ‘the only natural economy, the only kind that makes sense, the only one that can lead to [[prosperity:번영]], because it is the only one that reflects the nature of life itself’. But although the free market system now seems more natural than nature, ironically it fails to value and maintain natural capital — our biggest source of wealth, crucial to all human life and [[flourishing:번영,풍요]] — and in consequence, industrial capitalism is eating itself from within.

14.title: Mini Test 2 5번 (112P)

14.passage: Setting effective goals motivates people to work hard and increases their chances of success. But what is an effective goal? The organizational psychologists Edwin Locke and Gary Latham developed an [[influential:영향력 있는]] theory. According to Locke and Latham, challenging and specific goals are the best if they are not [[overly:과도하게]] difficult. Challenging goals encourage effort, [[persistence:끈기, 지속성]], and concentration. In contrast, goals that are too easy or too hard can [[undermine:약화시키다, 손상시키다]] motivation and therefore lead to failure. Dividing specific goals into [[concrete:구체적인]] steps also leads to success. If you are interested in running the Boston Marathon, for instance, your first goal might be gaining the [[stamina:체력]] to run 1 mile. When you can run a mile, you can set another goal and thus build up to running the 26-mile marathon. Focusing on concrete, short-term goals [[facilitates:촉진하다, 용이하게 하다]] achieving long-term goals.

15.passage: Economists have developed techniques for measuring such things as prices, [[supply and demand:공급과 수요]], money supplies, rates of inflation, and employment. This study of the creation, [[distribution:분배]], and consumption of goods and services is known as economics. The economy, however, is just one part of society, and each individual in society decides whether to buy an American car or a Japanese [[import:수입품, 수입하다]], whether she or he is able to handle the mortgage payment on a dream house, and so on. Whereas economists study price and availability factors, sociologists are interested in the social factors that influence a person’s economic decisions. Does peer pressure result in buying the large [[flashy:호화로운]] car, or does concern about gas mileage lead to the purchase of a fuel-efficient or hybrid vehicle? What social and cultural factors [[contribute:기여하다, 공헌하다]] to the differences in the [[portion:비율, 몫]] of income saved by the average wage earner in different societies? What effect does the unequal [[allocation:할당, 배분]] of resources have on social interaction? These are examples of the questions sociologists seek to answer.
